newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Growing Serbian protests weaken Milosevic.
newsitem.headline: Growing Serbian protests weaken Milosevic.

text.p: Serbian protests against socialist election rigging have taken on a new dimension, giving urgency to international efforts to end the crisis between President Slobodan Milosevic and his opposition.

For the past month protests against Milosevic's refusal to reinstate anulled local elections have drawn big crowds. At the weekend 250,000 people, the biggest crowd yet, gathered in the capital and protests spread to 30 towns across Serbia.
The sheer scale of the discontent has raised the stakes considerably.
"Both have to reach a compromise quick or it will be too late," a Western diplomat said.
Diplomats were fearful that some protesters were raising their expectations for radical change, making it harder for opposition leaders to appease them with a compromise.
Milosevic has already made concessions. The popular independent Belgrade radio station B92 was legalised after being shut down briefly to stop its broadcasts of protests.
On Sunday a court in the southern city of Nis ordered the election commission to hand back victory won in the November elections to the opposition Zajedno (Together) coalition.
Belgrade's recent street protests brought echoes of the revolutions which broke the back of communist rule in eastern Europe in 1989-90.
But diplomats cautioned against comparing the intricacies of Balkan politics with what happened elsewhere in the region.

Opposition leaders are not ready to take over the immense burden of running Serbia, diplomats believe. "There is no one single strong opposition leader waiting in the wings to succeed Milosevic," one said.
"Milosevic is still by far the most popular leader in the country. The local election result vote was not so much for the opposition as it was against his local party hacks," another said.
Serbia has already been involved in two wars in Croatia and Bosnia since 1991 which sapped its energies, making it ready for change but wary of violence, other diplomats argue.
They fear too much pressure on Milosevic could cause a bloodbath in Serbia, a threat the authorities are quietly keen to foster as a deterrent to the opposition.
The peaceful and carnival nature of the protests is preventing police hardliners who would like to crack down on the demonstrators.
Milosevic came to power in the late 1980s after police excercised restraint during his "Yoghurt Revolution", so called because protesters threw yoghurt to demonstrate at rallies.
People power then proved too big to resist. The same phenomenon is working against Milosevic now.
Authoritative sources said he had crisis meetings with leaders of the ruling socialist party last week.

"One could easily imagine he had some harsh words to say. Not only did they lose elections for him, not only were they totally unprepared for defeat but they also bungled the aftermath and tarnished his image," a diplomat said.

The United States, spearheading Western condemnation of Milosevic, warned Serbia could be cut off from economic aid and funds unless he opened himself to democratic processes and endorsed election results.

"Coming from the United States that is a very strong position which gives Milosevic a clear signal of our support for the democratic process," U.S. envoy John Kornblum said after meeting Zajedno leaders in Geneva.
The threat would render useless his efforts to secure the Dayton peace accord at the cost of alienating Bosnian Serbs.
Far worse for Milosevic, some countries have started questioning whether he is really needed to implement the Dayton accord since his reputation "is as bad as can be."

"He will quickly have to choose between his party hacks who let him down and are restraining him to save their own skins or join the democratic process with the backing of his people," a Western political analyst said.
